analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes federal college aid, raising the maximum Pell Grant to $6,000 and adding loan forgiveness for public-service work.
analysis.headline: The House passed the higher education rewrite 221-199 on March 30, 2006, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died on the Senate calendar when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill renews and revises the main federal higher education law. It raises the maximum Pell Grant to $6,000 for low- and middle-income students, creates a $1,000 bonus grant for students who complete a rigorous high school program, and expands loan forgiveness for nurses, teachers, first responders, and other public-service workers [S4]. It also simplifies the student aid application, treats foster and homeless youth as financially independent for aid purposes, and cancels the loans of spouses and parents of 9/11 victims [S4]. It extends the rule requiring schools to draw at least 10% of revenue from non-federal sources to all colleges, while folding for-profit colleges into a single eligibility definition [S4]. The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote; the Senate left it on the calendar and it expired [S7].
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income and working-class college students gain through a higher maximum Pell Grant, year-round grant eligibility, and a simplified aid form [S4]. Students who enter public-service careers — nurses, early childhood educators, teachers in low-income communities, first responders, librarians — gain a new federal loan forgiveness program [S4]. Foster youth and homeless youth gain by being counted as independent students, which usually raises their aid [S4]. Families of 9/11 victims gain loan cancellation [S4]. For-profit colleges gain a single, uniform eligibility definition, though they remain barred from institutional aid programs [S4]. Federal guaranteed student loan lenders gain from continued reauthorization of the guaranteed loan channel [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students, 9/11 families, for-profit colleges, loan lenders

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $6,000 for academic years 2007-08 through 2013-14 and allows a second Pell award within a single year for students attending school year-round [S4].
Establishes a $1,000 Pell Grants Plus award for first-year students who completed a rigorous high school program, with a $1,000 continuation award for a 3.0 GPA in year two [S4].

Creates federal student loan forgiveness for service in areas of national need, covering early childhood educators, nurses, foreign language specialists, librarians, teachers in low-income communities, first responders, child welfare workers, and others [S4].
Directs the Secretary of Education to cancel the federal student loan debt of spouses and parents of people killed or permanently disabled in the September 11, 2001 attacks [S4].

Simplifies the student aid application with an EZ-FAFSA form and treats foster youth, orphans, wards of the court, and homeless or unaccompanied youth as independent students, which typically increases their aid eligibility [S4].

Requires accreditors to confirm that colleges publicly disclose whether they deny transfer credit based solely on the sending school's accreditation, and requires colleges to publish transfer policies, making it harder to strand transfer students' credits [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the reauthorized grant, work-study, and institutional aid programs, including the higher Pell authorization [S4]. The loan forgiveness expansions and the continued federal guarantee of private student loans add federal costs through the loan system [S3]. Colleges bear new reporting duties, including a published college affordability index, public explanation when tuition rises faster than twice inflation, task forces for the worst offenders, and fines up to $25,000 for data failures [S4]. Students who exhaust 18 semesters of Pell eligibility or use Pell for more than one year of remedial coursework lose eligibility under the bill's new limits [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and some long-enrolled students

drawbacks.text: The bill caps lifetime Pell eligibility at 18 semesters (27 quarters) and limits Pell use for noncredit or remedial courses, including English language instruction, to one academic year — provisions that fall on the least-prepared students the grants exist to help [S4].

The college affordability 'index' is a reporting and publicity tool: schools whose tuition rises faster than twice inflation must explain themselves and convene task forces, but nothing in the bill caps tuition or claws back money except fines for bad data [S4].

The bill creates a Teacher Incentive Fund for performance-based pay and directs states to develop merit-based compensation systems, a shift teachers' organizations have long argued undermines experience-based pay and pushes pay decisions toward test scores [S4].

As originally introduced, the bill would have repealed both the 90/10 rule (requiring for-profit colleges to get at least 10% of revenue outside federal student aid) and the 50% distance-education limit; the version that passed instead extends 90/10 to all schools, but the rewrite still folds for-profit colleges into a single eligibility definition for federal aid programs [S2].

The bill narrows the drug-offense penalty so it affects eligibility only for convictions during enrollment, but it still excludes from aid students subject to involuntary civil commitment after incarceration for a sexual offense, and makes most Freely Associated States' students ineligible for federal aid [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The student-aid core is genuinely valuable: a larger Pell Grant, year-round awards, loan forgiveness for public-service work, and a simpler application all go to people of modest means. The honest weaknesses are that the Pell increase is an authorization Congress must still fund; the lifetime and remedial-course limits cut against struggling students; the affordability provisions shame high-tuition schools without constraining them; and the bill keeps federal loan money flowing through private guaranteed lenders rather than the government's own cheaper Direct Loan channel. It is a mixed bill whose student-aid benefits are real but whose structural choices favor the existing loan industry and expand for-profit colleges' formal access to federal aid.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 221-199 in March 2006, but the Senate never took it up — it simply sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended in January 2007, so it never became law.

narrative.text: Rep. John Boehner introduced the bill on February 8, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S7].
The committee reported the bill as amended on September 22, 2005, on a 27-20 vote, and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S7].
The House debated it under a rule limiting amendments and passed it on March 30, 2006, by a recorded vote of 221-199 (Roll Call 81) [S8].
The vote split sharply by party: 207 of 230 Republicans voted yes against 18 no, while only 14 of 201 Democrats voted yes against 180 no; the one Independent voted no [S8].
Rep. George Miller, the committee's ranking Democrat, offered a substitute amendment in the nature of a replacement that was rejected on a recorded vote during floor debate [S7].

The Senate received the bill on April 4, 2006, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — it never came to a vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing student loan and for-profit college arrangements stayed exactly as they were, and the bill's Pell increase never took effect through this vehicle. Students and borrowers waited until the next Congress, which passed a different higher education law in 2008 that included larger aid increases and student-lender reforms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The student loan industry kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split overwhelmingly by party: 207 of 230 Republicans yes versus 14 of 201 Democrats yes, with the lone Independent voting no [S8].

industries.industry: Federal guaranteed student loan lenders and guaranty agencies
industries.note: The bill reauthorizes the Federal Family Education Loan program, keeping federal loan money flowing through private lenders and guaranty agencies rather than shifting it to the government-run Direct Loan program, which lends to students at lower cost. Because the bill died, this entrenched middleman system continued unchanged [S3].

The bill folds for-profit colleges into a single eligibility definition covering all Higher Education Act programs, formalizing their access to federal student aid, while barring them from institutional aid programs and extending the 90/10 revenue rule to all schools. The introduced version would have gone further, repealing the 90/10 rule for them entirely [S2].

They gain from reauthorized Pell, campus-based aid, and institutional grant programs that bring in students and revenue, but face a published college affordability index, required explanations when tuition rises more than twice as fast as inflation, task forces for the worst offenders, and fines up to $25,000 for data failures [S4].
